title: KEY INSIGHT: the TypeScript errors are mostly NOISE — and the real serializer bugs are INVISIBLE to the compiler
scenario: Triaged all 50 'property does not exist' errors (38 TS2339 + 12 TS2551). Only 4 were real runtime bugs. So the compiler is crying wolf 92% of the time — which is exactly why nobody triages this list. WORSE: the genuinely broken code is often NOT flagged at all, because the wrong code and the wrong type agree with each other (see BH-0201, where the compiler flags the ONE correct line and stays silent on the three broken ones). title: GSTR-1 silently DROPS every overdue invoice from the GST return — and GSTR-3B includes them, so the two filings cannot reconcile
scenario: generateGSTR1 filters the invoice query with `status: { not: InvoiceStatus.OVERDUE }`. The InvoiceStatus enum (schema.prisma:8634) is PENDING / PARTIALLY_PAID / PAID / OVERDUE — there is NO CANCELLED or VOID value. So this filter can never exclude a voided invoice (there is no such thing); it can ONLY exclude legitimately-issued invoices that the customer has not yet paid on time. Concretely: an interstate invoice dated 5-Jul for Rs 1,00,000 + 18% IGST (Rs 18,000). The customer pays late. The invoice flips to OVERDUE. The July GSTR-1 now omits it entirely — b2b, HSN summary and totals all under-report by Rs 1,00,000 of taxable turnover and Rs 18,000 of IGST — even though the GST was legally charged and is due. Meanwhile generateGSTR3B (same file, ~line 269) applies NO status filter, so it DOES include that invoice's tax. The two returns for the same period therefore disagree by exactly the overdue invoices, which is precisely the kind of GSTR-1 vs GSTR-3B mismatch that triggers a departmental notice. CRITICAL POINT ON REACHABILITY (the skeptic's main line of attack): the admin-only POST /invoices/update-overdue endpoint is never called by any page and there is no cron — but OVERDUE is NOT dead, because it is set as a routine SIDE EFFECT of ordinary operations: createInvoice sets OVERDUE outright if dueDate has already passed (invoice.service.ts:277), and BOTH recordPayment (:685) and updateInvoice (:574) recalculate status via calculateInvoiceStatus (:198-224), which returns OVERDUE for any past-due invoice that isn't fully paid. Recording a partial payment on a late invoice — an everyday event — is enough to flip it. So overdue invoices accumulate naturally and are then silently excluded from every GSTR-1 run. FIX: drop the status filter from generateGSTR1 (payment status is irrelevant to outward-supply reporting — GST is due on the invoice, not on the collection), and add a real CANCELLED status if voiding is what was actually intended.

title: You can receive MORE fabric back from the mill than you ever sent — and it becomes real stock

FIX: bound qtyReceivedMeters against qtySentMeters (allow a sane tolerance for over-delivery, reject the rest), and reject negative computed shrinkage.

scenario: PROVED BY EXECUTING THE REAL SCHEMA. This is not an ordinary mismatch; it is unsatisfiable. The Zod schema accepts sampleType in [DEVELOPMENT, FIT, PRE_PRODUCTION, PRODUCTION, PHOTO_SHOOT]. The Prisma enum SampleType is [FIT_SAMPLE, PHOTO_SAMPLE, PRODUCTION_SAMPLE, PP_SAMPLE, SIZE_SET_SAMPLE, SHIPMENT_SAMPLE]. **The intersection is EMPTY.** There is no string on earth that satisfies both: anything Zod accepts, Prisma rejects, and vice-versa. So POST /api/samples cannot succeed for ANY input — not one sample type, not ever. SampleForm.tsx defaults to 'FIT_SAMPLE' (matching Prisma and the frontend types), and validateBody hard-fails it with a 400 before the controller is ever reached. I executed the real schema against the real form default and it returned FAIL with `sampleType: Invalid option: expected one of "DEVELOPMENT"|"FIT"|"PRE_PRODUCTION"|"PRODUCTION"|"PHOTO_SHOOT"`. The same parse ALSO fails on customerId and requiredDate, which the schema requires and the form never sends. LIVE-DB CONFIRMATION: samples = **0 rows**. The entire Sample Tracking module — a core garment-industry workflow — has never produced a single record and could not have. FIX: rewrite the Zod enum to mirror the Prisma enum exactly, and drop the required customerId/requiredDate (or make the form send them). Then confirm with `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM samples;` after one manual create.

title: DORMANT: deleting a pending delivery note destroys the finished goods — stock is deducted at creation and never given back

title: DORMANT: embroidery receipt has no upper bound and partial receipts OVERWRITE each other instead of adding up
scenario: TWO bugs in one function. (1) NO UPPER BOUND: nothing compares quantityReceived against sendOut.quantitySent. Send 100 m out for embroidery, receive 1000 m: `tx.fabric_stock.create({quantityAvailable: data.quantityReceived})` cheerfully materialises 1000 m of brand-new embroidered stock from a 100 m send-out. 900 m of fabric conjured from a typo. (2) PARTIAL RECEIPTS OVERWRITE: the re-entry guard only blocks status RECEIVED or CANCELLED — a PARTIALLY_RECEIVED send-out can be received again and again, and each call SETS quantityReceived to that call's number rather than adding to the running total. Two legitimate partial receipts of 50 m + 50 m against a 100 m send-out leave quantityReceived = 50 (the last call's value) and the status stuck on PARTIALLY_RECEIVED forever — the send-out can never be closed, and the record understates what came back. DORMANT: both endpoints 400 on every call today (BH-0180 zod-drift). But the routes ARE registered and the frontend pages DO call them — so **the day you fix that schema mismatch, this S1 goes live**. Fix them together. FIX: bound quantityReceived + quantityDamaged against quantitySent minus what has already been received; use {increment} rather than an absolute set.

title: DORMANT: a customer can REJECT an entire shipment and the system still records it as DELIVERED
scenario: recordPOD accepts deliveryStatus in [DELIVERED, PARTIAL, REJECTED] plus shortageQty and rejectionReason, dutifully stores them on dispatch_pods — and then, two lines later, updates the delivery note with a HARDCODED status: 'DELIVERED', regardless of what was submitted. So a customer rejecting 100% of a shipment leaves the delivery note reading DELIVERED, and the finished_goods_stock that was decremented at note-creation (BH-0236) is never credited back for the rejected or short quantity: the goods are physically back in your warehouse but permanently absent from stock. title: DORMANT: the over-dispatch guard is computed per-SKU and then thrown away — you can ship 200 Smalls against an order for 100 S + 100 M
scenario: THREE defects in one function. (1) The over-dispatch check builds a per-SKU map keyed styleId-colorId-sizeId, then immediately FLATTENS it into one grand total and compares that against the order's total across ALL SKUs. An order for 100 Small + 100 Medium (200 total) accepts a delivery note for 200 Small — double what was ordered in that size, zero Medium — because the order-wide total isn't exceeded. The per-SKU limits are computed and discarded. (2) The stock deduction does findFirst with `colorId: item.colorId || undefined` — when colorId is falsy, Prisma DROPS the key from the where-clause entirely (rather than matching null), so the deduction can land on the WRONG COLOUR's stock row for the same style/size. (3) If no single location holds enough stock, the deduction is SILENTLY SKIPPED ('still allow dispatch') — so a delivery note can be created with zero physical stock backing it, and nobody is told. It also reads-then-writes an absolute quantity instead of using {decrement}. FIX: enforce the per-SKU map you already built; use `colorId: item.colorId ?? null`; fail loudly (or split across locations) instead of skipping the deduction.

title: CLEAN — and IMPORTANT: embroidery sendOut/cancelSendOut is EXEMPLARY. It is the model the broken code should copy
scenario: The most useful negative result of the run, because it proves the team already knows how to do this correctly — the bugs are inconsistency, not ignorance. embroidery-stock.service.ts `sendOut()` does EVERYTHING right: wrapped in prisma.$transaction; uses atomic {decrement} (not read-then-absolute-write); BOUND-CHECKS the requested quantity against sourceStock.quantityAvailable before sending; and correctly calls ensureMaterialRecord + syncStockLevelQuantity per the mandated material-sync pattern in CLAUDE.md. And `cancelSendOut()` is the direct counter-example to this report's most dangerous pattern: it CORRECTLY REVERSES the stock with an atomic {increment}, inside a transaction, gated to the SENT status only. **Compare that with cancelChallan (BH-0214) and deleteDeliveryNote (BH-0236), which flip a status and never give the stock back.** Point the fix pass at cancelSendOut as the reference implementation. ALSO VERIFIED CLEAN: dispatch_pods.deliveryNoteExtId carries a real @@unique, so a double-submitted POD is caught by the database (P2002) — that race is DEAD, not a finding. dispatchDeliveryNote/assignTransport do omit the status from their where-clause, but every consequence is an idempotent field overwrite with no stock or money impact — not reported. Samples deliberately track no stock consumption (qtySent is a plain integer with no FK to any stock table), so there is nothing to reconcile — by design, not a bug. NOTE ON STRUCTURE: there is NO dispatch/deliveryNote/asn service file at all — every bit of that logic lives directly in dispatch.controller.ts, which is why the stock handling there never picked up the helpers the service layer uses.

title: Fabric issued to a cutting batch can NEVER be released — the restore code is dead, and 'Cancel' doesn't cancel
scenario: THE FOURTH INSTANCE of the reverse-without-reversing pattern (after cancelChallan BH-0214, deleteDeliveryNote BH-0236, and the processing send). TWO defects: (1) DELETE's restore is DEAD CODE. deleteCuttingBatch restores fabric via `Number(existing.fabricIssued || existing.fabricConsumed || 0)` — but fabricIssued is only ever written by completeCuttingBatch, and fabricConsumed only when a lay exists. Delete is permitted ONLY when there are no lays and the status is PENDING/ON_HOLD/IN_PROGRESS — under exactly that precondition both fields are always null/0. So the restore always computes 0 and gives nothing back, even though creation already deducted the entire lot (BH-0242). (2) CANCEL ISN'T CANCEL. cancelCuttingBatch is a byte-for-byte copy of holdCuttingBatch: it sets status to 'ON_HOLD' and writes 'CANCELLED:' into the remarks text. There IS no CANCELLED state — the Prisma CuttingBatchStatus enum is only PENDING/IN_PROGRESS/COMPLETED/ON_HOLD. It never touches fabric_stock. So a cancelled batch is INDISTINGUISHABLE from a held one (same 'On Hold' badge), can be silently un-cancelled via resumeCuttingBatch, and once it has lays it can never be deleted either — its fabric is locked away forever. FIX: add a real CANCELLED status; make cancel release the issued fabric (copy `cancelSendOut()` — BH-CLEAN-09); and fix the restore to read the quantity actually issued.

title: Clicking 'Generate Transfer Slip' twice in Finishing DOUBLES your finished-goods stock — and the button stays clickable forever
scenario: No concurrency needed; one extra click does it. generateTransferSlip's ONLY guard is `issue.status !== 'COMPLETED'` — and the endpoint never advances the status, so that guard stays satisfied permanently. There is no check for an already-existing slip (no @unique on the column), and the frontend button is gated only by a transient loading flag, never disabled after success. Finish 500 pcs of style S1/Red/M: click once -> slip TS-0001 created, finished_goods_stock goes 0 -> 500. Click the still-live button again (impatience, or just revisiting the page later) -> slip TS-0002, a second REAL dispatch document, and finished_goods_stock -> 1000. The system now believes 1,000 pieces exist when only 500 were ever made — and both slips are dispatchable. The same missing-guard exists in stitching's generateTransferSlip. Compounding it, the stock write is a read-then-absolute-write (`quantity: existing.quantity + sku.finishedQty`) rather than an atomic {increment}, so two finishing issues for the same style/colour/size can also silently clobber each other. title: NOTHING on the production floor bounds a quantity — you can cut, stitch and finish more pieces than were ever issued
scenario: A systemic hole across all three production stages. Not one of them compares the recorded quantity against what was issued. Size M with toCut=100: Lay 1 gives 50, Lay 2 gives 100 -> cutQty = 150, fifty over the hard cap, no error anywhere. (2) STITCHING: recordDailyOutput writes goodQty/defectQty straight from the request body with zero aggregation check against stitching_issue_skus.issuedQty. title: 'Receive from Cutting' and 'Receive from Stitching' are rubber stamps — any shortage you report is silently thrown away
scenario: Both receive endpoints accept a detailed reconciliation payload and then IGNORE IT ENTIRELY. receiveFromCutting destructures `skuReceived` from the body and never reads it again — it only flips the status to RECEIVED and stamps the transfer slip. The frontend types declare skuReceived[].shortageQty / excessQty / remarks, so the UI clearly intends to reconcile what physically arrived against what was sent — but nothing is ever compared or written. receiveFromStitching is the same: `receivedQty` is required by the schema and never read by the controller. CONSEQUENCE: the system ALWAYS believes 100% of what was sent arrived exactly as planned. If cutting sends 500 pieces and stitching physically receives 480, the 20 missing pieces are invisible — no shortage recorded, no variance, no alert. The one place in the whole production chain where you would catch theft, loss or miscounting is a no-op. (Note: BH-0176 already covers the fact that Receive-from-Stitching 400s on every call; this is the bug UNDERNEATH it — fixing the 400 still leaves you with a rubber stamp.) DORMANT. title: Your real JWT signing key and database password are committed to git — and rotating them in place will NOT remove them
scenario: VERIFIED MYSELF (values never printed — I checked only that the keys exist and are populated). `git ls-files` shows these are all TRACKED: .env, backend/.env, backend/.env.local, backend/.env.backup.1766396133123, frontend/.env. The committed backend/.env contains a populated JWT_SECRET (65 chars — a real, strong key) and a populated DATABASE_URL (59 chars, with embedded DB credentials). They were first committed in 235aab8e and are still present at HEAD. IMPORTANT NUANCE: .gitignore DOES list `.env` (line 7) — but .gitignore has no effect on files already tracked. The rules are there; they were added too late, and nobody untracked the files. WHAT IT ACTUALLY MEANS — calibrated honestly: the repo is PRIVATE (verified via gh: varunsharda1987/garment-erp, visibility PRIVATE), so this is NOT an internet-exposed leak, and I am not going to alarm you as if it were. But the JWT signing key is what proves a token is genuine. Anyone who has ever had read access to this repo — any current or former collaborator, anyone who cloned it, any CI service or tool you granted access — holds that key permanently, and can mint a valid token for ANY user including ADMIN. And because the value lives in git HISTORY, changing the secret on the server does not remove it: the old key stays in every clone forever unless the history is rewritten. NOT AS BAD AS IT LOOKS ON ONE POINT: AI_API_KEY is present but only 2 characters long — an empty placeholder, not a real third-party key. No billable credential is exposed. FIX, in order: (1) rotate the JWT secret and the DB password NOW (this invalidates the committed values for future use — do this first, it's the part that actually protects you); (2) `git rm --cached backend/.env .env backend/.env.local frontend/.env backend/.env.backup.*` and commit, so they stop being tracked going forward; (3) only then consider rewriting history (git-filter-repo / BFG) if the repo has ever been shared beyond people you'd trust with the credentials anyway.

title: The JWT secret falls back to a hardcoded string — if the env var is ever missing, anyone can forge an ADMIN token
scenario: `const JWT_SECRET = process.env.JWT_SECRET || 'your-secret-key-change-in-production';` This one line signs AND verifies every token in the system. If JWT_SECRET is ever unset in ANY environment that runs this code — a fresh clone, CI, a staging box, a Docker container that forgot the env var, a dotenv load that runs in the wrong order — the server silently switches to signing with that literal, well-known string. No error, no warning; it just works, insecurely. At that point anyone who knows the string (it is in your source code, and it is a common placeholder that appears in countless tutorials) can mint a token with `role: 'ADMIN'` that passes authenticateToken and authorize() on every protected route in the app. The current production box does set a real secret, so this specific path is not active today — but it is a silent, catastrophic failure mode that triggers on a config mistake rather than an attack. FIX (one line, and it makes the whole class impossible): throw on startup if JWT_SECRET is unset. `if (!process.env.JWT_SECRET) throw new Error('JWT_SECRET is required');` A server that refuses to boot is infinitely better than one that boots with a public key.

title: Firing someone doesn't lock them out — deactivating or demoting a user does not revoke their existing token
scenario: authenticateToken verifies the JWT's signature and expiry and then TRUSTS THE PAYLOAD as-is: `req.user = decoded`. It never re-reads the user from the database, so it never checks whether that user is still active or still has the role the token claims. There is no token blacklist, no session table, and no token-version claim to invalidate against. CONSEQUENCE: an admin deactivates a departing (or compromised) employee via DELETE /api/users/:id, which sets isActive = false. That person's already-issued bearer token KEEPS WORKING — with their old role — for up to JWT_EXPIRES_IN, which defaults to **7 days**. The same applies to demotion: strip someone's ADMIN role and they remain an admin, as far as every request is concerned, for a week. This is the gap between what the admin THINKS they did (revoked access) and what actually happened (nothing, for 7 days). FIX: either re-check isActive/role from the DB inside authenticateToken (one indexed lookup per request — fine at this scale), or add a tokenVersion column to users, put it in the JWT, and bump it on deactivate/role-change so old tokens fail verification.

-> authorize(role) then trusts req.user.role, which came from the token, not the database
user.controller.ts deleteUser()/updateUserRole() only flip DB columns; nothing invalidates issued tokens
evidence: const decoded = verifyToken(token); req.user = decoded; next();   // no DB re-check of isActive or role
const JWT_EXPIRES_IN = process.env.JWT_EXPIRES_IN || '7d';   // the length of the window
skeptic_verdict: CONFIRMED S2 — grep-verified that no blacklist, session store or token-version mechanism exists anywhere in the codebase.

title: The approval routes have no role checks — and their own comments claim they do
scenario: Authentication is solid across this app (see BH-CLEAN-11: 1,198 of 1,205 routes require a valid token). AUTHORIZATION is where it breaks down: only 18 of 127 route files use authorize() at all. So ANY authenticated employee — of ANY role — can perform actions the code itself documents as restricted. The gap is worst on approvals and pricing, which are exactly the decisions roles exist to protect: (1) **GRN approve/reject** (PATCH /api/grn/:id/approve) — the route is doc-commented `@access Private (QC, ADMIN)` but has NO authorize() call. Anyone can accept or reject incoming goods against a PO. (2) **Credit-note and debit-note approve / cancel / delete** — any authenticated user can approve or permanently delete a financial document that adjusts a customer's balance. (3) **Purchase-order create/update/delete/send/cancel** — every one doc-commented `@access Private (PURCHASE, ADMIN)`; none enforces it. Anyone can raise or cancel a PO. (4) **Processor rate cards and fabric-costing rates** — anyone can change the per-processor cost rates that feed every cost sheet and PO price. THE TELLING PART: this module KNOWS the pattern. The same purchaseOrder.routes.ts file DOES call authorize('ADMIN','PURCHASE',...) on its /stats and /by-source GET routes, and the sibling unified-po.routes.ts enforces authorize() properly. So role gating exists and is used — it was simply never applied to the base CRUD and the state transitions. The doc comments are a map of the intent; the code just doesn't implement it. FIX: add authorize(...) to the mutating and approval routes, using the roles the comments already specify. The roles are defined and the middleware exists.

title: Anyone registering can request the ADMIN role for themselves — bounded, but a social-engineering foothold
scenario: POST /api/auth/register is (correctly) public, and its Zod schema accepts a client-supplied `role` from the full enum — INCLUDING 'ADMIN' — which the controller stores verbatim. THIS IS NOT AN AUTH BYPASS, and I want to be precise about that: the account is created with `isApproved: false` and cannot log in until an existing admin approves it via POST /api/users/:id/approve, which IS properly gated with authorize(UserRole.ADMIN). The real risk is social engineering: an admin reviewing the pending-users queue sees a row already labelled with the ADMIN role, with nothing to indicate the applicant chose it themselves. One distracted click and it's granted. FIX: don't accept `role` from a registration request at all — default every self-registration to the lowest role, and make role assignment a separate, deliberate admin action.

title: Uploaded files are served to anyone with the URL, and /uploads reflects any Origin with credentials
scenario: TWO related hardening gaps on the same mount. (1) fileAccessMiddleware reads FILE_ACCESS_MODE, which is NOT SET in any .env — so it defaults to 'public': every file under /uploads/* is downloadable by anyone with the URL, no token required. Impact TODAY is low (it holds ~1,000 product photos and some UUID-named catalogue PDFs that look meant to be shareable), but it is a single switch governing 'any future upload type' — the day someone uploads scanned invoices or signed contracts, those inherit public access silently. (2) The /uploads CORS middleware reflects the request's Origin header verbatim with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, bypassing the explicit origin whitelist the rest of the API correctly enforces. Not exploitable today because auth is a Bearer token, not a cookie — but it becomes directly exploitable the moment any cookie-scoped secret touches that path. FIX: set FILE_ACCESS_MODE explicitly (don't rely on a permissive default), and apply the same origin whitelist to /uploads that the rest of the API already uses.

title: CLEAN AND IMPORTANT: your AUTHENTICATION is genuinely solid — 1,198 of 1,205 routes require a valid token, and the 7 that don't are correctly public
scenario: The most reassuring result of the entire audit, and it deserves to be stated as plainly as the bugs. A script parsed all 127 route files and every one of the 1,205 route registrations, resolving whole-router `router.use(authenticateToken)`, path-scoped `router.use('/prefix', authenticateToken)`, and inline middleware (and correctly handling the multi-router files that a naive pass miscounts). RESULT: **exactly 7 routes are reachable without authentication, and all 7 SHOULD be** — POST /auth/register and POST /auth/login (both behind a rate limiter: 5 failed attempts per 15 min in production, skipSuccessfulRequests), the 4 /health endpoints, and GET /api/ai/status (which returns only whether an AI provider is configured — no ERP data). **No unauthenticated data access or mutation exists anywhere in the API surface.** ALSO VERIFIED CLEAN: (a) PASSWORDS — bcrypt with 10 rounds used consistently for both hash and compare; no plaintext password logging anywhere; no ==/=== password comparisons; and EVERY response-facing users query uses an explicit Prisma `select` that excludes the password hash (I had the auditor check every findMany/findUnique/findFirst call site individually, because the serializer would happily pass a hash through to the frontend if one ever slipped into a select). (b) TENANCY — schema.prisma has NO tenant/org/company_id field anywhere; this is a genuinely single-tenant internal ERP by design, so cross-tenant IDOR does not apply and getById-by-id-alone is CORRECT here, not a bug. I am explicitly recording that as a non-finding so nobody 'fixes' it later. (c) RATE LIMITING present on auth. (d) CORS is an explicit origin whitelist (except /uploads — BH-0256). (e) helmet configured with a real CSP and HSTS in production. (f) the global error handler does NOT leak stack traces in production — it returns a generic message plus a correlation requestId. CONCLUSION: the front door is locked. The problems are the key being in git (BH-0251/0252) and the missing role checks INSIDE the building (BH-0254) — not an open door.

title: ALL FOUR dashboards are structurally broken — every KPI reads zero, including money the backend correctly calculated
scenario: VERIFIED MYSELF at both ends. The backend returns a FLAT object: `res.json({ data: { monthlyCollections, totalReceivables, totalPayables } })` — there is NO `stats` wrapper. Every dashboard reads `dashboardData?.stats?.X ?? 0`. `stats` is undefined, so EVERY TILE FALLS BACK TO ZERO — including the values the backend went to the trouble of computing correctly. This is not an empty-database artefact; it is a response-shape mismatch that would show zeros no matter how much real data you have. AFFECTED (all four role dashboards): (1) ACCOUNTS — Outstanding Invoices, Overdue Amount, GST Payable, Monthly Collections, all four aging buckets, and the Recent Invoices table. With Rs 18,50,000 genuinely outstanding and Rs 4,20,000 overdue, the accounts team sees Rs 0 across the board and nobody chases collections. (2) SALES — Active Orders, Monthly Revenue, Recent Orders, Pending Quotations. (3) PRODUCTION — cutting/stitching/finishing queue counts and the active work-order table, even though the backend computes them correctly. (4) GENERAL (the default dashboard for every role and for admins) — Total Orders, Active Work Orders and Active Customers are never even computed by the backend, and sit next to tiles that ARE real, so a viewer cannot tell which zeros are true. WHY THIS IS S1 AND NOT COSMETIC: a dashboard that ERRORS makes you distrust it. A dashboard that confidently reports Rs 0 outstanding makes you stop collecting money. FIX: one line per endpoint — wrap the payload in `stats`, or read the flat keys in the frontend. Then compute the KPIs that were never implemented (recentInvoices, agingData, overdueAmount, gstPayable, ...).

title: The dashboards display FABRICATED growth percentages — '+12% vs last month' is a hardcoded literal, computed from nothing
scenario: VERIFIED MYSELF by grep. Every role dashboard glues an invented trend badge onto its tiles. No period-over-period comparison is computed ANYWHERE in the codebase — these are literals in the JSX: GeneralDashboard Monthly Revenue -> `trend={{ value: 12, direction: 'up', label: 'vs last month' }}`. AccountsDashboard -> `+8% vs last month` and `+3%`. SalesDashboard -> `+12% vs last month` and `+5%`. ProductionDashboard -> `+5% vs last week`. And several tiles are pure invention end to end, with no data behind them at all: Production Efficiency = the literal string '87%'. Sales Conversion Rate = '68%'. Collection Rate = '78%'. title: 'Monthly Revenue' can never see a late payment — it filters on when the INVOICE was created, not when the money arrived

Run the dashboard on 31 July: the invoice is PAID, but its createdAt (25 June) is before July's start, so it is EXCLUDED from July's revenue. It was also excluded from June (it wasn't PAID then). **The Rs 5,00,000 never appears in Monthly Revenue in ANY month.** Any invoice paid in a later month than it was raised — which is most of them — silently vanishes from the revenue figure forever. And the app already knows better: the accounts endpoint in the SAME FILE correctly aggregates `payments` by `paymentDate`. So two dashboards, read by two different managers, will disagree about how much money came in. title: GSTR-3B claims Input Tax Credit from PURCHASE ORDERS, not from goods actually received — you can claim ITC on goods that haven't arrived
scenario: The ITC section of GSTR-3B sums CGST/SGST/IGST from `purchase_orders` where the status is SENT / ACKNOWLEDGED / PARTIALLY_RECEIVED / RECEIVED — with NO check against any goods-receipt record. So: a PO for Rs 10,00,000 (Rs 1,80,000 GST) is emailed to a supplier and marked ACKNOWLEDGED on 28 June; the goods don't physically arrive until August. June's GSTR-3B claims the full Rs 1,80,000 as available ITC. Under Section 16 of the CGST Act, ITC may only be claimed once the goods or services are ACTUALLY RECEIVED. Claiming on PO acknowledgement is an over-claim: it risks the return being rejected on audit, plus interest and penalty on the excess credit. Note the status list literally includes SENT — a PO that has merely been emailed. FIX: derive ITC from goods_receiving_notes (actual receipt), not from PO status. If a PO is only partially received, claim only the received portion.

title: The CSV importer splits on every comma — one comma inside a style name silently shifts every column after it
scenario: The parser is `lines[i].split(',')` with no quote awareness, then assigns values to headers positionally. A perfectly ordinary row — `COS009,ABC Corp,Fabindia,S,"Kurta Set, Blue With Piping"` — gets cut at the comma INSIDE the quoted style name. The parser now has 6 values for 5 headers: styleName becomes 'Kurta Set', and ' Blue With Piping' either falls off the end or shifts into the next column. Because styleName is optional, NO validation error fires. The row imports 'successfully' with silently wrong data, and the uploader is told it worked. title: Saving a style DELETES AND RECREATES its SKU variants with new row IDs — real, but I OVERSTATED the damage and am correcting it

title: SYSTEMIC AMPLIFIER: your API client silently RETRIES POSTs up to 3 times on any server error — so one click can apply a stock change FOUR times
scenario: VERIFIED BY ME AT SOURCE. This is the most dangerous single line of configuration in the app, because it AMPLIFIES every non-idempotent write in the entire system. `axiosRetry(api, { retries: 3, retryCondition: (error) => axiosRetry.isNetworkOrIdempotentRequestError(error) || error.response?.status === 429 || error.response?.status >= 500 })`. Read that last clause carefully: it retries on ANY 5xx **regardless of HTTP method**. The library's own `isNetworkOrIdempotentRequestError` deliberately limits retries to GET/HEAD/PUT/DELETE precisely because POST is not safe to repeat — and this config overrides that safety by adding a method-blind condition. It ALSO retries on a raw network drop, which is the classic killer: the server commits the write, the connection dies before the response arrives, and the client cheerfully resends. THE CONCRETE DAMAGE, combined with BH-0281: 'decrease greige lot by 10 m' hits a transient 500 or a dropped connection. The retry fires. The endpoint is a non-idempotent read-modify-write (read current, compute new, write ABSOLUTE), so the delta is applied AGAIN. With `retries: 3`, one user action can deduct 40 m instead of 10 m — and the user sees only the final 200 OK and a success toast. No error, no indication. THIS IS WHY IT IS S1: it converts every transient blip into silent data corruption, across every non-idempotent POST in the app — stock adjustments, GRN approvals, challan issues, payment recording. It also defeats the frontend's own protection: the Apply Adjustment button IS correctly disabled during the request, but the retry happens INSIDE the axios layer, below the button. FIX: restrict retries to idempotent methods — drop the bare `status >= 500` clause and let `isNetworkOrIdempotentRequestError` do its job. That single edit removes the amplifier from every write in the system.

-> any non-idempotent POST is applied up to 4x. See BH-0281 for the endpoint this corrupts.

title: Manual stock adjustment is a read-then-absolute-write — the endpoint the retry bug (BH-0280) turns into silent corruption
scenario: Both the greige adjustment (greige-stock.service.ts:658-728) and the near-identical fabric one (fabric-stock.controller.ts:976-1044) do: findUnique the current quantity -> compute `newQty = current +/- delta` in JavaScript -> write `quantityAvailable: newQty` as an ABSOLUTE value. No transaction, no optimistic lock, no atomic `{increment}/{decrement}`, and nothing that makes a repeat call a no-op. On its own this is the familiar lost-update race and, for a small team, would be S3. **What lifts it to S2 is BH-0280**: the API client silently retries this POST on any 5xx or dropped connection, so the delta gets re-applied with NO second user action and NO error shown — 'decrease by 10 m' becomes an actual decrease of 20 m (or 40 m), plus a duplicate ADJUSTMENT_OUT audit row for a single user action. title: A fully-consumed greige lot can stay 'AVAILABLE' forever — the status is decided on an unrounded float, then the quantity is silently rounded to zero
scenario: VERIFIED BY ME AT SOURCE, and the mechanism is precise. consumeGreigeStock subtracts in plain JavaScript floats, then decides the lot's status from that raw result: `status: newReserved + newAvailable <= 0 ? 'EXHAUSTED' : 'AVAILABLE'`. But the column it writes to is `Decimal(10,2)` — so **Postgres rounds the stored quantity to 2 decimal places, while the status was already decided from the unrounded float.** Consume a 199.9 m lot in three issues of 66.3 + 66.3 + 67.3 and the float residue is **+2.84e-14** — not zero. So `<= 0` is false, the status stays AVAILABLE, and the quantity is then rounded to **0.00** on write. You are left with a self-contradictory row: **quantityAvailable = 0.00, status = AVAILABLE.** And because getGreigeStock filters on `status: 'AVAILABLE'` with **no quantity > 0 filter**, that phantom lot is returned forever — it shows on the Greige Available Stock page as usable stock that does not exist, and it can never flip to EXHAUSTED. WHY IT HASN'T BITTEN YET (the reviewer's sharpest observation): the live DB has 26 real CONSUMPTION transactions across 7 lots consumed in multiple steps — the path is genuinely exercised — but **every quantity so far happens to be a multiple of 0.25**, which is exactly representable in binary floating point. The bug fires the first time anyone books a quantity that isn't a clean binary fraction — i.e. almost any ordinary 2-decimal value like 66.3 or 33.45. It is a loaded gun, not a hypothetical. FIX: do the comparison on the rounded value (or use Prisma Decimal arithmetic end-to-end), and add a `quantityAvailable > 0` filter to the availability query as a belt-and-braces guard.

title: When fabric arrives at a different width than planned, the CAD updates the width but KEEPS the old marker length — so you reserve the wrong amount of fabric
scenario: VERIFIED BY ME AT SOURCE. A CAD (marker) is a physical layout: at width W, a marker of length L yields N garments. **The marker length is only valid at the width it was laid out for** — on wider fabric more pieces fit across, so the same N garments need a SHORTER marker. createProductionCADFromStock correctly sets `cutableWidth: stockWidth` (the width actually received) but then does `cadMeters: sourceCAD?.cadMeters` — copying the marker length verbatim from a CAD measured at a DIFFERENT width. The per-piece consumption (cadAverage) is therefore left describing the old width. WORKED FROM A REAL LIVE ROW: source CAD at 52" with cadMeters 10.5 m, margin 0.2, 5 pieces per marker -> cadAverage = 10.7/5 = **2.14 m/piece** (matches the DB exactly). The next lot arrives at 58" — an entirely routine event; this module literally generates -2"/-4"/-6" width options *because width varies by lot*. The new CAD records 58" but still carries cadMeters 10.5 and cadAverage 2.14. At approval, cad-approval.controller.ts:24 does `quantityNeeded = cadAverage * orderQuantityPcs` — and for the real orderQuantityPcs = 3,200 on that row, that **reserves 3,200 x 2.14 = 6,848 m of real fabric stock** against a marker that no longer describes the fabric. A wider roll needs less; a narrower one needs more and leaves cutting short. THE DAMNING PART: the code **computes and stores `widthVariance` and `variancePercent`** — it KNOWS the width changed — and a repo-wide grep confirms those fields are **only ever displayed. They gate nothing.** The system measures the problem and ignores it. FIX: recompute cadMeters/cadAverage for the new width (or refuse to copy a CAD across a width change), and make widthVariance actually block approval beyond a tolerance.

title: A unique constraint that protects NOTHING: all 11 brand_categories rows are exempt from it, because Postgres treats NULLs as distinct
scenario: VERIFIED BY ME AGAINST THE LIVE INDEX AND THE LIVE ROWS. This is the most insidious kind of bug, because it gives false confidence: the schema declares `@@unique([customerId, brandName, category, subCategory, subSubCategory])`, which looks like solid protection against duplicate brands. It is not. `subCategory` and `subSubCategory` are nullable, and **Postgres never treats two NULLs as equal in a unique index** — so two rows with the same customer + brand + category and NULL sub-categories do NOT violate the constraint. Both inserts succeed. I checked the actual index (`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... btree (customerId, brandName, category, subCategory, subSubCategory)` — a plain unique index, NOT the Postgres-15 `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` variant) and then the actual data: **all 11 of your 11 brand_categories rows have subCategory = NULL.** So the constraint currently protects **zero rows**. It is decorative. title: 16 of 77 composite unique constraints silently DO NOT ENFORCE (nullable columns) — a real hole, but NOT yet breached (I corrected my own over-claim)
scenario:
VERIFIED BY ME, AND THEN VERIFIED AGAINST THE LIVE DATA. This generalises BH-0298 into a systemic defect. **Postgres never treats two NULLs as equal in a unique index.** So any composite `@@unique([...])` containing a NULLABLE column silently stops enforcing uniqueness for every row where that column is NULL. I parsed all 77 composite uniques in your schema: **16 of them contain at least one nullable column.** The worst offenders sit on your LIVE stock tables:
  - **greige_stock** — `@@unique([greigeId, procurementId, greigeWidth, qualityGrade, supplierId, processorId, sourceChallanId])` with **FOUR nullable columns**. **22 of your 61 greige lots have a NULL procurementId**, and are therefore entirely unprotected.
  - **fabric_stock** — same shape (nullable procurementId, embroideryId).
  - **fabric_width_cad** (149 rows) — FIVE nullable columns in its unique.
  - **processor_rate_card** (956 rows) — FOUR nullable. Duplicate rate cards would mean the price you charge depends on which row wins.
  - **Eight SKU tables** (cutting_batch_skus, cutting_lay_skus, transfer_slip_skus, stitching_issue_skus, finishing_issue_skus, order_item_breakup, work_order_breakup, sale_order_items) all use `@@unique([parentId, colorId, sizeId])` with **colorId nullable** — so a style with no colour can have duplicate size rows, and SKU-level dedup silently fails.
**IT HAS ALREADY HAPPENED.** I tested rigorously — grouping by EVERY column in each constraint, so a legitimate second lot from a different challan would NOT be miscounted:
  - **greige_stock: 1 true duplicate group** — GRG-0017 (63", grade A): **two rows identical across all seven constrained columns**, holding 15,797.9 m between them. The database should have rejected the second insert. It didn't.
  - **fabric_stock: 3 true duplicate groups.**
**AND GRG-0017 IS ALREADY ONE OF YOUR CORRUPTED MATERIALS** — it is one of the two carrying a NEGATIVE stock level (BH-0294). So this is a SECOND, INDEPENDENT mechanism feeding the same corruption: BH-0296 splits the *materials* ledger, and this splits the *stock lot* itself. FIX: for each of the 16, either make the columns NOT NULL with a sentinel value, or use Postgres 15's `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` on the index, or add a partial unique index covering the NULL case. **Start with greige_stock and fabric_stock — they are live and already breached.** This trap is completely invisible in the Prisma schema, which is why it survived.

That is verified and real. **What I got WRONG:** I claimed the constraint had ALREADY been breached — that GRG-0017 had two identical greige lots the DB should have rejected. It does not. title: Your database enforces NOTHING about values: ZERO check constraints across 576 money and quantity columns — which is why the impossible negative stock was allowed in
scenario: VERIFIED BY ME AGAINST THE LIVE DATABASE. I queried `pg_constraint` for user-defined CHECK constraints across the entire public schema. **The answer is ZERO.** Not one. Meanwhile there are **576 numeric columns whose names contain quantity / qty / amount / price / cost / rate / total / meters / percent** — every money and quantity value in your ERP. **None of them has a single database-level guarantee.** A price can be negative. A quantity can be negative. A percentage can be 5,000. The database will accept all of it without complaint. THIS IS NOT ACADEMIC — IT IS EXACTLY WHY BH-0294 HAPPENED. Two `stock_levels.quantity` rows currently hold **negative** values (−7,589.6 and −5,869.5). A physically impossible state. **The database should have refused those writes and had no rule telling it to.** Every safety guarantee in this system lives in application code — and this report is 300+ findings demonstrating that application code fails. The database is your last line of defence, and it is currently unmanned. **AN IMPORTANT AND REASSURING DETAIL:** the negatives exist ONLY in `stock_levels` (the derived cache). `greige_stock.quantityAvailable`, `greige_stock.quantityConsumed` and `fabric_stock.quantityAvailable` all have **zero** negative rows. That is a third independent confirmation that the specialized tables hold the truth and only the derived cache is corrupt — which is precisely what REPAIR_PLAN.md relies on. FIX: add CHECK constraints on the columns that genuinely cannot be negative — stock quantities first, then prices and percentages. Start with `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` on stock_levels and the specialized stock tables. **These are cheap, they are enforced no matter which code path writes, and they would have caught this corruption at the moment it happened instead of months later.**

title: ROOT CAUSE of the wrong-unit corruption: syncStockLevelQuantity defaults the unit to 'PIECE' — so any caller that forgets to pass one records fabric in pieces
scenario: VERIFIED BY ME AT SOURCE. The mandated sync helper declares `unit: string = 'PIECE'` as a DEFAULT PARAMETER. So any of its 13 callers that creates a new stock_levels row without explicitly passing a unit silently records that material in **PIECE**. That is how a poplin measured in metres ended up with a stock_levels row reading **-5,869.5 PIECE** (BH-0294) while both `materials.unit` and `greige_stock.unit` correctly say METER. A default of PIECE for a system whose primary materials are FABRIC (metres) and GREIGE (metres) is precisely backwards — and because it is a *default*, it fails silently rather than erroring. This is a one-line root cause with a one-line fix: **remove the default and make `unit` a required parameter**, so a caller that forgets is caught by the compiler rather than by a corrupt row six months later. THE SAME FUNCTION HAS A SECOND, RELATED HOLE: `syncStockLevelQuantity` performs its decrement with **no floor check and no sufficiency check** — unlike the `decreaseStock()` method in the very same file, which correctly validates `currentQty.lt(decreaseQty)` before subtracting. That missing check is how the quantity went NEGATIVE. **The correct guard exists in the same file, ten lines away, and this function doesn't use it** — the recurring theme of this entire report.

title: The OTHER direction: processor consumption never syncs at all — which is why GRG-0034 OVERSTATES stock by 17,080 m

VERIFIED BY ME AGAINST THE LIVE DATA. This is on real paperwork that has already travelled with goods. The printed challan renders each item row with its OWN unit (correct), but the TOTAL row at the bottom prints the CHALLAN HEADER's unit — and that header unit is set by `unit: input.unit || Unit.PIECE` in challan.service.ts:152. But this is a document that legally states what left your building, and it currently contradicts itself. title: Your stock audit trail is ONE-SIDED: every outflow is logged, no receipt EVER is. The ledger cannot explain where 145,851 metres came from
scenario: VERIFIED BY ME AT SOURCE AND AGAINST THE LIVE DATA. `createGreigeStock` — the path by which greige stock ENTERS your business — creates the stock lot, calls ensureMaterialRecord and syncStockLevelQuantity, and then **never writes a greige_stock_transaction row.** Consumption is logged. Transfers out are logged. Adjustments are logged. Processor-returns are logged (the code even has a RECEIPT type, used ONLY for goods coming back from a processor). **The original receipt is not logged at all.** THE LIVE PROOF: greige_stock_transaction contains ONLY outflows — 26 CONSUMPTION rows and 20 TRANSFER_OUT rows — and **nets to -100,561 metres.** Meanwhile you actually hold **145,851 metres**. The audit trail literally cannot account for a single metre of the stock you own. WHY THIS MATTERS, in three ways: (1) **You cannot audit a quantity.** If a lot's figure looks wrong — and this report proves 95,727 m of them are — there is no receipt record to check it against. You cannot reconstruct how any lot reached its current number. (2) **You cannot use the transaction log to verify the repair.** I had hoped it could serve as an independent check on REPAIR_PLAN.md. It cannot; it is not a ledger, it is a debit list. (3) **A stock ledger that records only what leaves is an audit and compliance gap** in its own right — for a business that sends goods to job workers on legal challans, there is no systemic record of what arrived. NOTE HOW THIS REINFORCES THE REPAIR: the lot rows themselves ARE internally consistent (BH-CLEAN-21: all 61 lots satisfy available + consumed = nominal). So the lots remain the only usable source of truth — which is exactly what REPAIR_PLAN.md rebuilds from. FIX: write a RECEIPT transaction in createGreigeStock (and the equivalent fabric/lace/thread paths), so the ledger balances and can be audited.

title: THE GREIGE GAP EXPLAINED: the sync helper SILENTLY DROPS a material's first receipt when no warehouse is supplied — and the main Add Greige Stock form never supplies one
scenario: THE COMPANION TO BH-0309, AND IT CLOSES THE GREIGE HALF. syncStockLevelQuantity's create-guard reads: `if (updateResult.count === 0 && change > 0 && warehouseId)`. **If warehouseId is falsy, no row is created — the receipt is silently discarded.** And when a row already exists, the where-clause scopes only by materialId, so the credit lands on *whichever* warehouse row happens to exist, not the one that physically received the goods. TWO LIVE RECEIPT PATHS HIT THIS: (1) **GreigeStockEntry.tsx — the primary 'Add Stock' page for greige — never sends a warehouseId at all.** It collects only a free-text `warehouseLocation` (populated from the warehouse *name*). So its sync call passes `undefined`. (2) fabric-stock.service.ts createStyleStock hardcodes `syncStockLevelQuantity(materialId, qty, undefined, 'METER')` — the DTO has no warehouseId field. THE FORENSIC PROOF, from GRG-0017: stock_movements records **two STOCK_IN receipts totalling +23,388.5 m** (12,596 on 16 Apr; 10,792.5 on 1 May). The ledger today says **−7,589.6**. Work it backwards: −7,589.6 + 3,756.9 + 3,833.7 (the two consumption debits) = **+1.00** — exactly the one legacy lot from January. **So the 23,388.5 m of receipts NEVER credited the ledger, while every consumption debit landed in full.** That is the precise mechanism of the negative balance: **credits dropped, debits applied.** Combined with BH-0305 (processor consumption never syncs, causing the GRG-0034 *over*-statement), all three directions of the corruption are now explained. FIX: make `warehouseId` required (the form must send it), and remove `&& warehouseId` from the create-guard so a receipt can never be silently dropped.

title: CLEAN: the manual Stock IN form — the path 22 of your lots came through — is CORRECT. The bugs are in the OTHER entry forms
scenario: A precise and useful boundary. There are several ways to add stock, and they are NOT equally broken. **StockInForm.tsx -> createStockIn/createBulkStockIn is SOUND**: it wraps stock_movements + stock_transactions + a **properly warehouse-scoped** stock_levels increment (find-or-create by {materialId, warehouseId}) + routeToSpecializedStock **all inside ONE prisma.$transaction**, and **warehouseId is REQUIRED** in both the backend DTO and the frontend form validation. routeToSpecializedStock correctly threads `tx` through and sets `skipMaterialSync: true` so the specialized write cannot double-credit. **This is the reference implementation** — the other entry forms should copy it. ALSO VERIFIED CORRECT: the nominal-vs-actual fold-length maths (`actualQty = nominalQty * foldLengthCm/100` when foldLengthCm < 100) is applied consistently in BOTH createGreigeStock and createStockIn, and it is the ACTUAL quantity that reaches both the ledger and the lot — no nominal/actual confusion. AND: the fabric_procurement CRUD controller (/api/procurement) has NO frontend caller at all — it is dormant. The live procurement rows are auto-created as a by-product of stock entry, hardcoded to status RECEIVED at the moment the lot is created, so **there is no separate 'mark as received' step and therefore no double-receipt or over-receipt exposure through the UI.** THE LESSON: the corruption is not 'stock entry is broken'. It is that **three different forms enter stock three different ways, and only one of them does it correctly.**

title: THIRD CORRECTION TO MY OWN REPAIR PLAN — caught by DRY-RUNNING it read-only. The rebuild as written would have DOUBLED the stock on 5 materials.
scenario: I stopped trusting my own plan and executed it read-only to see exactly what it would produce. It exposed a flaw that reading it never would have. THE FLAW: the plan said rebuild stock_levels per material from the lots. But FIVE greige masters have TWO materials rows each (GRG-0009 and GRG-0009-RAW), and BOTH point at the SAME greigeId. So a per-material rebuild credits the full lot total to EACH of them. GRG-0009 would have been set to 24,637.5 on BOTH rows — showing 49,275 m of stock where 24,637.5 m exists. Same for GRG-0017. THE PLAN WOULD HAVE DOUBLED THE STOCK ON 5 MATERIALS. THE CORRECTED ORDER, which is deliberately NOT the obvious one: (a) resolve the 5 duplicate materials pairs FIRST, picking the survivor by checking which is actually referenced (and NOT assuming -RAW is disposable — for GRG-0029 and GRG-0049 the -RAW row holds the ONLY correct figure); (b) THEN rebuild, so each greige maps to exactly one material and the lot total is credited exactly once; (c) skip the ~24 materials with no lots rather than creating zero rows; (d) re-run the dry run and confirm the total matches SUM(greige_stock.quantityAvailable) before committing. THE LESSON, and it is the third time: READING A PLAN IS NOT THE SAME AS RUNNING IT. Two of my three destructive errors were in the REMEDIATION, not the diagnosis. The dry-run output is now published in REPAIR_PLAN.md so the developer can see exactly what each row would become before touching anything.

title: The Greige export WORKS — and then tells the user it failed. Every single time.
scenario: VERIFIED BY ME AT SOURCE. handleExport builds the spreadsheet and calls `XLSX.writeFile(...)`, which **succeeds — the .xlsx file lands in the user's Downloads folder.** The very next line then does `handleApiSuccess('Export successful', `${result.totalRecords} greige masters exported`)` — but **`result` is never defined in that scope** (only `response` exists). That throws a ReferenceError, which is caught by the surrounding catch block, which shows the user: **'Failed to export greige masters: result is not defined'**. So the export works perfectly and the user is told it broke. 100% reproducible, on the live 54-row Greige Masters list. WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: a user seeing that error will retry (getting a second file), or conclude the feature is broken and stop using it, or report it as a bug that a developer then cannot reproduce — because the file *is* there. A success reported as a failure wastes more time than an honest failure. FIX: one word — use `response` (or just drop the count from the message).

title: Saving a processor rate card fires ~1,400 sequential database round-trips — and the page resubmits the ENTIRE matrix on every click
scenario: THE FIRST PERFORMANCE BUG FOUND IN THIS AUDIT, and it is one the user feels every single time they use the feature. `saveProcessorRateMatrix` loops over every rate cell and, for each one, issues: a `findFirst` to look for an existing rate, then `updateRateWithHistory`, which does a `findUnique` with four nested includes and **opens its OWN `prisma.$transaction`** containing two updates and two creates. That is roughly **eight sequential round-trips PER CELL**. THE REAL MATRIX SIZE, from your live data: one processor's PRINTING matrix has **172 cells** (43 greiges x 4 slabs), and there are four printing sub-types at 172 cells each — **956 rate-card rows in total.** And the frontend makes it worse: ProcessorRateCardPage **does not diff against what it loaded** — it rebuilds the whole matrix from every row on screen and **resubmits ALL of it on every Save**, even if the user changed one cell. So a single Save click on that matrix = **172 x 8 + ~86 (the shrinkage loop) ≈ 1,460 sequential DB round-trips.** MEASURED, not guessed: running just **two** of the ~8 per-cell queries sequentially across the real 172-cell matrix took **728 ms** (4.23 ms/query) on a local database with near-zero network latency. The full save path runs roughly four times that many queries per cell, projecting to **several seconds locally — and comfortably past 10 seconds on any hosted/managed Postgres**, where per-round-trip latency is typically 3-10x a loopback connection. AND ONCE AGAIN, THE RIGHT PATTERN IS NEXT DOOR: the CAD planning controller in the same codebase correctly uses `deleteMany` + `createMany` for its size breakdowns instead of a per-row loop. title: The .passthrough() FALSE-CONFIDENCE TRAP — an outer .passthrough() does NOT protect nested item schemas, and 19 schema files rely on it
scenario: THE GENERALIZABLE LESSON BEHIND BH-0316, worth more than the single bug. Zod's `.passthrough()` preserves unknown keys — but **only on the object it is called on.** It does NOT propagate into nested schemas. So a schema shaped like `z.object({ ..., items: z.array(itemSchema) }).passthrough()` looks safe, and IS safe at the top level — while `itemSchema` underneath is still SILENTLY STRIPPING every key it does not declare. This is exactly how BH-0316 (delivery note colorId/sizeId) happens, and it recurs in the same file: asnSkuSchema (dispatch.schema.ts:138-142) declares colorId/sizeId/**quantity**, while the controller reads `plannedQty: sku.plannedQty` (dispatch.controller.ts:755-759) — a name that the schema never declares — and asn_skus.plannedQty is NOT NULL (schema.prisma:6472). So any ASN created WITH a SKU breakdown throws too. **19 schema files use .passthrough()** (dispatch, dyeing, embroidery, fabricCosting, fabricCostingRun, fabricGreige, fabricProcurement, genericTrim, grn, laceCosting, laceStock, lookup, machinePart, printing, processorRateCard, production, sample, supplier, trimMasters) — every nested item schema under any of them deserves the same check, and grn.schema.ts in particular is worth auditing first because GRN items carry the quantities that become stock. FIX: for each nested item schema, diff its declared keys against what the controller actually reads from the item. ALSO IN THIS FILE, the reverse drift: createASNSchema marks plannedDispatchQty / cartonsPlanned / requestedShipDate `.optional()` (dispatch.schema.ts:153-155) while asn_applications requires all three NOT NULL (schema.prisma:6441-6443) — so a form built to the letter of the schema would 500. title: You cannot edit your processor rate cards AT ALL — every Save returns 400. Three independent causes, on a LIVE feature with 956 rate rows.
scenario: A LIVE, HEAVILY-USED FEATURE THAT CANNOT SAVE. `RateCellSchema` (processorRateCard.schema.ts:37-42) declares the rate field as **`rate: z.number().nonnegative()`** — REQUIRED. The frontend (ProcessorRateCardPage.tsx:288-292) pushes **`{ greigeId, slabId, ratePerMeter: rate }`** — it sends **`ratePerMeter`, and never sends `rate` at all.** The route DOES apply `validateBody(saveMatrixSchema)` (processor-rate-card-v2.routes.ts:68-71), and `rates: z.array(RateCellSchema).min(1)` is mandatory — so Zod throws a required-field error on EVERY cell and the request dies with a 400 before the controller ever runs. The feature is BROKEN, not DESTRUCTIVE — and the difference matters enormously. (The 956 rows were created through some other path — a seed or an earlier schema version.) FIX: rename `rate` -> `ratePerMeter` in RateCellSchema, relax `slabId` from `.uuid()` to `.string()`, and fix the shrinkages shape. Roughly a 15-minute change that restores an entire screen.

title: YOUR QUALITY GATES ARE DECORATIVE — the documented pre-commit hook NEVER RUNS, and 6 of the 9 checks that do run can never block a commit
scenario: THIS IS WHY 367 BUGS ACCUMULATED. title: HONEST LIMIT: even if you un-muzzle the alignment checker, it would still miss most of this audit — it covers 14% of routes and never looks at nested schemas or frontend payloads
scenario: A CORRECTION TO MY OWN REASONING, and I am writing it down because the tempting conclusion is wrong. Having found that the alignment check is warning-only (BH-0338), I was about to tell you "turn it on and it would have caught the whole Zod-drift class." **I ran it to check. It would not have.** Its own summary says **"Total routes checked: 76"** — and this repo has **528 POST/PUT/PATCH routes.** That is **14% coverage.** And its METHOD is narrower still: it compares the Zod schema against what the controller **destructures from `req.body` at the top level**. It therefore CANNOT see: (a) **nested item schemas** — the `items[].colorId` strip that makes every Delivery Note create crash (BH-0316), the `skuOutputs[].sizeName` that kills Cutting (BH-0324), the GRN override fields (BH-0323); (b) **frontend-payload mismatches** — the rate card sending `ratePerMeter` while the schema demands `rate` (BH-0322), which is invisible to any backend-only check because the schema and the controller agree with *each other* perfectly; (c) **double-validation** — the cost sheet re-parsing with a second schema (BH-0314). title: YOU CANNOT CREATE A USER. And when an admin changes someone's password, it is silently discarded — success toast, password unchanged.
scenario: THE BEST FIND OF THE RUN, and a textbook demonstration of why a backend-only checker can never see this. **CREATE IS A THREE-WAY DISAGREEMENT.** The form (UserForm.tsx:63-71) sends `{ email, password, firstName, lastName, phone, role, department }`. The controller (user.controller.ts:103) destructures `{ email, password, firstName, lastName, phone, role, department }` — **the form and the controller agree perfectly.** But `createUserSchema` (user.schema.ts:37) sits between them and requires **`name: z.string().min(1, 'Name is required')`** — and declares **neither `firstName` nor `lastName`.** The route applies it (`router.post('/', authorize(ADMIN), validateBody(createUserSchema), createUser)`). So: Zod throws *"Name is required"* -> **400.** And even if it did not, Zod would have **stripped firstName and lastName**, so the controller's own guard — `if (!email || !password || !firstName || !lastName) throw new ValidationError(...)` (user.controller.ts:106) — would throw anyway. **Two independent failures. Creating a user through the UI is impossible.** **AND THE UPDATE PATH IS WORSE, BECAUSE IT FAILS SILENTLY.** `updateUserSchema` (user.schema.ts:48-54) is a plain `z.object` with **no `.passthrough()`** and declares only `{ email, name, phone, avatar, isActive }`. The controller reads `password` — it is always `undefined`. **An administrator who edits a user to reset their password gets a success message and the password does not change.** That is a security-relevant silent failure: someone believes a compromised credential has been rotated when it has not. title: THE METHOD IS PROVEN: the check nobody wrote found 11 new bugs in one pass — including 6 completely dead features — in forms nobody had looked at
scenario: THE VINDICATION OF BH-0340, AND THE STRONGEST ARGUMENT IN THIS REPORT FOR ONE SPECIFIC PIECE OF TOOLING. title: A SYSTEMIC 400-GENERATOR: `z.string().datetime()` REJECTS every date your UI produces. 131 validators vs 68 date pickers.
scenario:
THE BIGGEST SINGLE BUG CLASS IN THE ENTIRE AUDIT, and I proved it against your own installed Zod rather than assuming. **Every `<input type="date">` in a browser emits `"2026-07-15"` — a date, with no time.** And `z.string().datetime()` demands a full ISO-8601 timestamp. I ran it against your actual dependency (zod 4.1.12):
```
.datetime() on "2026-07-15"  -> REJECTED
.datetime() on a full ISO ts  -> PASS
.optional() still rejects ""  -> REJECTED   <- optional does NOT save you
```
**`.optional()` only permits `undefined` — it does NOT permit a present-but-wrong value**, which is why several of these fail even where the field is marked optional. THE SCALE: **131 `.datetime()` validators across 20 schema files**, against **68 `<input type="date">` fields** in your pages. Every intersection is a guaranteed 400. CONFIRMED INSTANCES SO FAR: sample `requiredDate` (kills create AND edit), sample `sentDate` (kills "Mark as Sent"), printing Process-PO `sentDate`/`receivedDate` (kills both "Send to Mill" and "Receive from Mill"). **AND HERE IS THE PROOF THAT IT IS DRIFT AND NOT DESIGN: Dyeing does the exact same thing through the exact same UI pattern and WORKS** — because `dyeing.schema.ts` uses a plain `z.string().optional()` for those fields. **The two sibling modules disagree, and only one of them functions.** FIX: replace `z.string().datetime()` with something that accepts a date — `z.coerce.date()` is the usual answer — everywhere a `<input type="date">` feeds it. This is a find-and-replace across 20 files that would resurrect a large number of features at once.

title: "Calculate Services" reads a localStorage key that NOTHING in the app ever writes — so it always sends an empty string and always 400s
scenario: A FEATURE THAT HAS NEVER WORKED, AND CANNOT. WorkOrderDetail.tsx:206 does `const userId = localStorage.getItem('userId') || '';` and posts `{ userId }`. **`localStorage.setItem('userId', ...)` does not appear ANYWHERE in the frontend codebase** — the key is never written. So `getItem` always returns `null`, the `|| ''` fallback always sends **an empty string**, and `calculateServicesSchema` (serviceRequirement.schema.ts:43-45) requires `userId: z.string().uuid()` — **which rejects it.** Every "Calculate Services" click 400s, and always has. **The correct value was available the whole time**: the app has a `useAuthStore()` that is used correctly elsewhere in the very same file. It would not be caught by a schema-vs-controller check, nor by a form-payload-vs-schema check that only compares *key names* — you have to notice that the *value* is structurally always empty. It is a good argument for the humblest possible check: **does any code path ever write the thing this code reads?**

title: THE SIGNATURE OF THIS ENTIRE CODEBASE: the form, the controller, the service and the database all agree with each other — and the ZOD SCHEMA is the lone outlier. Almost every fix is "fix the schema."
scenario: THE PATTERN BEHIND ~25 BROKEN FEATURES, and it is the most useful sentence in this report for whoever does the fixing. In case after case I traced the same shape: **the form sends X. The controller reads X. The service's DTO declares X. The Prisma column is X. And the Zod schema — sitting between the form and the controller — demands Y.** The schema is the only component that disagrees with everything else. **THE ROLL-CALL:** users (form+controller say `firstName`/`lastName`; schema says `name`) · orders (form+controller comment say `totalQuantity`+`breakup`; schema says `quantity`) · samples (UI+Prisma+controller say `FIT_SAMPLE`; schema says `FIT` — zero overlap) · external-process (form+controller+service say `sentQty`; schema says `quantity` — and the type enum has its words transposed) · greige stock edit (form+service DTO+frontend type say `purchaseCost`; schema says `rate`) · embroidery stock (controller+service still on the old design the schema abandoned) · stock adjustment (form says `quantity`; schema says `adjustmentQuantity`) · rate cards (form says `ratePerMeter`; schema says `rate`) · CAD (form says `cadRowId`; schema says `cadId`). **WHY THIS MATTERS PRACTICALLY:** (1) **The fix is almost always the schema, not the form** — do not "fix" the UI to match the schema, or you will break the controller behind it. (2) It explains why nobody caught these: **every existing check compares the schema to the CONTROLLER, and both of those are... no, wait — that is the point: the schema disagrees with the controller too, and the checker that would notice covers only 76 of 528 routes** (BH-0340). (3) **It tells you the schemas were never executed.** A schema whose enum has the words transposed (`PIECE_EMBROIDERY`), or whose enum shares not one value with the database, has demonstrably never validated a single real request. **These files were written from a design document, not from the running system, and never reconciled.** THE RECOMMENDATION FOLLOWS DIRECTLY: **generate the enums from Prisma** (that kills the sample, external-process and status-enum classes outright), **replace `z.string().datetime()` with `z.coerce.date()`** (that kills the 131-validator class, BH-0348), and **extend the alignment checker to all 528 routes and make it block** (BH-0338). Three mechanical changes that between them address the large majority of the broken features in this report.

orders: form + the controller's own comment say totalQuantity+breakup; schema says `quantity`
samples: UI+Prisma+controller say FIT_SAMPLE; schema says FIT — ZERO overlap
external-process: form+controller+service say sentQty; schema says quantity — and the type enum is TRANSPOSED (PIECE_EMBROIDERY vs EMBROIDERY_PIECE)
greige stock: form + service DTO + frontend type say purchaseCost; schema says rate
CONCLUSION: the schemas were written from a design doc, never executed, never reconciled
THEREFORE: fix the SCHEMA, not the form — "fixing" the UI to match would break the controller behind it
THREE MECHANICAL FIXES: generate enums from Prisma; z.string().datetime() -> z.coerce.date(); extend the alignment checker to all 528 routes and make it block
evidence: In ~25 broken features, the schema is the ONLY layer that disagrees with the others
An enum with its words transposed (PIECE_EMBROIDERY) and an enum sharing zero values with the DB (sample types) are proof these schemas never validated a real request
PRACTICAL: fix the schema, never the form — the controller behind it already agrees with the form
THREE mechanical changes (enums from Prisma; coerce.date; extend+enforce the checker) address the majority of the broken features
skeptic_verdict: CONFIRMED S2 — a synthesis rather than a new defect, but it is the finding that turns ~25 separate tickets into three mechanical changes, and it tells the developer which side of each mismatch to fix. That is worth more than any individual bug in this report.

title: STRESS-TESTING MY OWN FIX #1: `z.coerce.date()` IS the right answer — I verified it end to end — but the naive find-and-replace still 400s, and my "131 broken" figure was loose
scenario:
I ATTACKED MY OWN RECOMMENDATION BEFORE THE USER SPENDS A DAY ON IT. **WHAT I VERIFIED, AND IT ALL HOLDS:** (1) `z.coerce.date()` accepts **both** `"2026-07-15"` (what every `<input type="date">` produces) **and** a full ISO timestamp — so one replacement handles every form. (2) **It returns a `Date` object, not a string** — the obvious way this fix could break things. So I checked: **no controller or service anywhere does a string operation** (`.split`/`.substring`/`.slice`/`.replace`/`.startsWith`) on any of these date fields. (3) The controllers instead call `new Date(x)` on them — **29 times** — and `new Date(<Date>)` is perfectly safe (it returns a copy). **So the fix is sound and will not break the code behind it.** **BUT HERE IS WHAT A NAIVE FIND-AND-REPLACE WOULD STILL GET WRONG — and it would look like the fix had failed:** `z.coerce.date().optional()` **REJECTS an empty string.** `.optional()` permits `undefined`, NOT a present-but-empty value. **Four of your forms send `''` for an optional date** — those would still 400 after the "fix", and the developer would reasonably conclude the whole approach was wrong. **The correct form is:**
```ts
z.preprocess(v => v === '' ? undefined : v, z.coerce.date().optional())
```
**AND A CORRECTION TO MY OWN NUMBER.** I said "131 `.datetime()` validators — every intersection is a 400." **That is loose, and it is the same inflation I criticised myself for earlier in this run.** The truth: **131 validators exist**, but not all are fed by a date picker — **12 places in the frontend send a full ISO string, and those already pass today.** What IS true is that date-only production dominates heavily: **55 explicit `toISOString().split('T')[0]` truncations and 43 files containing `<input type="date">`, versus 12 full-ISO senders.** So the class is large and real — but I have **confirmed** a specific set (samples ×2, printing ×2, stitching/finishing), not all 131. **Fix the class; do not quote 131 as a bug count.**
trace: VERIFIED: z.coerce.date() accepts BOTH "2026-07-15" AND a full ISO timestamp -> one replacement covers every form
RISK CHECKED: it returns a Date, not a string. Grepped for .split/.substring/.slice/.replace/.startsWith on date fields in controllers+services -> ZERO hits
VERIFIED SAFE: controllers call new Date(x) on these fields 29 times; new Date(<Date>) returns a copy — no breakage
THE TRAP: z.coerce.date().optional() REJECTS "" — optional allows undefined, not a present-but-empty value
-> 4 forms send '' for an optional date; a naive replace would STILL 400 there, and look like the fix had failed
CORRECT FORM: z.preprocess(v => v === '' ? undefined : v, z.coerce.date().optional())

MY NUMBER WAS LOOSE: 131 validators exist, but 12 frontend senders use full ISO and already pass. Date-only dominates (55 truncations + 43 files with date pickers vs 12 full-ISO) — but 131 is not a bug count.
evidence: z.coerce.date() PASSES on both "2026-07-15" and a full ISO string — verified against the installed zod 4.1.12
ZERO string operations on date fields anywhere in controllers or services -> returning a Date object is safe
z.coerce.date().optional() REJECTS "" -> the naive fix still 400s on the 4 forms that send an empty date
The correct pattern is z.preprocess(v => v === '' ? undefined : v, z.coerce.date().optional())
HONEST SCOPING: 131 is the validator count, NOT the bug count. 12 senders already pass.
skeptic_verdict: CONFIRMED — the fix survives the stress test, with one real gotcha that would have made it look broken, plus a correction to my own inflated framing. This is exactly the check that was worth running before the user spent a day on it.

title: STRESS-TESTING MY OWN FIX #3: "just turn the checker on" WOULD RECREATE THE EXACT FAILURE I DIAGNOSED. It needs a ratchet, not a switch.
scenario: THE MOST IMPORTANT SELF-CORRECTION OF THIS ITERATION, because my advice would have failed in the same way the original decision did. I recommended: *extend the schema-controller checker from 76 routes to all of them, and make it block.* **Now read the comment that disabled it in the first place** (smart-check.js:117-119): *"don't block commits **for now since there are legacy mismatches**."* **The team did not disable enforcement out of laziness. They disabled it because turning it on would have blocked every commit until a pile of pre-existing violations was fixed.** So if the user follows my advice — extend coverage from **76 to the ~411 routes that actually have a `validateBody`**, and flip it to blocking — and it surfaces a significant number of violations, **nobody can commit anything until all of them are fixed.** The predictable outcome is that someone flips it back to warning-only, adds a comment saying *"for now"*, and **the codebase is exactly where it started.** I would have caused a repeat of the very failure I spent an iteration diagnosing. **THE CORRECT RECOMMENDATION IS A RATCHET, NOT A SWITCH:** **(1)** Extend the checker's coverage to all ~411 validated routes — but **first run it in report mode and write the current violations to a baseline file.** **(2)** Make it block **only on violations that are NOT in the baseline** — i.e. any NEW or NEWLY-TOUCHED mismatch fails the commit, while the legacy pile is tolerated. **(3)** Burn the baseline down over time; the file shrinks and can never grow. **This is the standard answer to "too many legacy violations to enforce", and it is the one thing that makes enforcement survivable on day one.** A blocking check that cannot be satisfied gets disabled. A blocking check that only catches *new* mistakes gets kept — and it would have caught every single Zod-drift bug in this report *as it was written*.

-> enforcement was disabled BECAUSE pre-existing violations made it unsatisfiable
SO: extending coverage 76 -> ~411 validated routes AND blocking would block every commit until the legacy pile is cleared
-> someone flips it back to warning-only "for now" -> the exact failure repeats
CORRECT: a RATCHET. (1) extend coverage, (2) baseline the existing violations to a file, (3) block only violations NOT in the baseline, (4) burn the baseline down
A blocking check that cannot be satisfied gets disabled. One that only catches NEW mistakes gets kept.

411 of 528 mutating routes have a validateBody — that is the checkable universe; the checker currently inspects 76 (18%)
A blocking check with an unsatisfiable backlog WILL be turned off. A baseline ratchet is the standard fix.
A ratchet would have caught every Zod-drift bug in this report at the moment it was written.
skeptic_verdict: CONFIRMED S1 — and it is a correction to my own recommendation, not a new bug. I diagnosed the ratchet failing open, then advised a fix that would have made it fail open again. The baseline ratchet is the version that survives contact with a real team.

title: A HOLE I CREATED IN MY OWN AUDIT: ~117 mutating routes have NO validateBody at all — and I marked several of those forms "CLEAN"
scenario: AN HONEST GAP IN MY OWN METHOD, and it means one of my clean bills was too generous. My form-payload-vs-schema check has a stated rule: *"if the route has no `validateBody`, nothing is stripped and nothing 400s -> CLEAN."* That is correct **for the bug I was hunting** — but it quietly hands a pass to routes that have **no request validation whatsoever.** THE NUMBERS: there are **528 POST/PUT/PATCH routes** and **411 `validateBody` calls** — so roughly **117 mutating routes accept raw, unvalidated `req.body` straight through to the controller.** Among them: `POST /challans/quick-issue` (the controller passes `req.body` directly through — and challans are LIVE, with 23 rows), the entire `stock-counts` create path, several lab-dip routes, and the `work-orders/:id/push-to-cutting` action. **These are not "clean" — they are unguarded.** They cannot suffer the Zod-strip bug for the simple reason that nothing is checking them at all, which is a *different* risk, not the absence of risk: a typo'd field name reaches Prisma directly, a negative quantity is accepted (and remember: **your database has zero CHECK constraints**, BH-0301), and a malformed payload becomes a 500 instead of a clean 400. **I am recording this because it is the kind of caveat that quietly inflates a clean bill.** When I say "42 forms audited, N clean," some of those clean bills mean *"validated and correct"* and some mean *"nothing is validating this at all."* **Those are not the same thing and should not be counted together.** RECOMMENDATION: add `validateBody` to the ~117 unguarded mutating routes — but do it **after** the schema-vs-form reconciliation (BH-0356), or you will simply create 117 new 400s.
