title: STOCK CAN BE CREATED FROM NOTHING: the Stock OUT endpoint has NO validation, and a negative quantity sails past the "insufficient stock" guard by making the balance GROW
scenario: THE MOST SERIOUS INTEGRITY HOLE I HAVE FOUND, and it is a three-part chain where each part is individually reasonable. **PART 1 — TWO DOORS, ONE ROOM, AND ONLY ONE IS LOCKED.** `POST /challans` is validated: `validateBody(createChallanSchema)`, whose item schema requires **`quantity: z.number().positive('Quantity must be positive')`**. But **`POST /challans/quick-issue` has NO `validateBody` at all** (challan.routes.ts:32) — and its controller does `quickIssueChallan({ ...req.body, issuedById: userId })`, spreading the **raw, unvalidated body**. And `quickIssueChallan` calls **the very same `createChallan()` service** the front door uses. **So the guard exists, and there is a second door straight past it.** This is not an obscure endpoint: **it is the one the Stock OUT form actually posts to** (challan.service.ts:44). **PART 2 — THE SERVICE HAS NO GUARD OF ITS OWN.** `createChallan()` simply does `input.items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.quantity, 0)` — no positivity check, no null check. **PART 3 — AND THE SAFETY NET IS FACING THE WRONG WAY.** `issueChallan()` deducts stock: `const newAvailable = Number(fabricStock.quantityAvailable) - qty;` followed by `if (newAvailable < 0) throw new Error('Insufficient fabric stock')`. **Feed it a NEGATIVE qty and `newAvailable` GROWS.** `available - (-500) = available + 500`. **The guard passes happily, and the update writes the inflated figure.** So one unvalidated POST with `quantity: -500` **manufactures 500 metres of cloth out of thin air** — and it does so through the *stock deduction* path, so it looks like ordinary activity. **AND THERE IS NO BACKSTOP:** your database has **ZERO check constraints** (BH-0301), so nothing below the application layer will refuse it. **HONEST STATUS: ARMED, NOT FIRED.** The Stock OUT form sends positive numbers, so this has not happened — the 23 live challans look normal. But the endpoint is authenticated-user-reachable, a frontend bug could send a negative, and nothing anywhere would stop it. **ALSO:** omit `items` entirely and `input.items.reduce(...)` throws a TypeError — a **500, not a clean 400.** FIX: put `validateBody(createChallanSchema)` on quick-issue (one line), and add the positivity guard **inside `createChallan()`** so no future route can bypass it.

title: 119 of your 528 mutating routes have NO request validation — and the split is inconsistent INSIDE a single router, so the unguarded ones are the stock-moving ones
scenario: THE SCALE BEHIND BH-0360, and the pattern is what makes it dangerous. Counted precisely (multi-line aware): **409 mutating routes carry a `validateBody`; 119 do not.** That alone would be a policy question. What makes it a bug is that **the guarded/unguarded split is inconsistent WITHIN THE SAME ROUTER**, and it is the *stock-mutating* actions that came out unguarded. In `challan.routes.ts`: `POST /challans` is **guarded**, while **`POST /challans/quick-issue`, `POST /challans/greige-outward`, `PUT /challans/:id/issue`, `PUT /challans/:id/receive` and `PUT /challans/:id/cancel` are ALL unguarded** — those five are precisely the actions that move stock. `processingBatch.routes.ts` has **zero `validateBody` across all four mutating routes**, and its controller spreads `...req.body` straight into the service (processingBatch.controller.ts:15). Also unguarded: `POST /fabric-processing`, `PUT /fabric-processing/:id/receive`, `POST /cad-planning/:styleId/sync-bom-fabric`, the lace lab-dip create/update, and `POST /production-runs/:id/split`. **WHY THIS PATTERN IS WORSE THAN "NO VALIDATION ANYWHERE":** a codebase with no validation at all is at least honest about it. Here, the *existence* of `createChallanSchema` gives every reader — and every reviewer — the reasonable belief that challan input is checked. **It is, on one route out of six.** AND A CAVEAT ON MY OWN AUDIT (BH-0359): my form-vs-schema sweep used the rule *"no validateBody -> nothing is stripped -> CLEAN"*. That was right for the bug I was hunting and **wrong as a safety verdict** — some of my "clean" bills mean *"correct"*, and some mean *"nothing is checking this at all."* This finding is the second kind. SEQUENCE THE FIX: add `validateBody` to these 119 routes **AFTER** reconciling the schemas with the forms (BH-0356), or you will convert 119 unvalidated routes into 119 fresh 400s.

title: THE ARCHITECTURAL LESSON: validation lives on the ROUTE, so every guarantee is one new route away from being void. Put the invariants in the SERVICE.
scenario: THE GENERALIZABLE FIX BEHIND BH-0360, and it is worth more than the individual bug. In this codebase **every safety guarantee is enforced at the route boundary** by `validateBody(schema)`. That means a guarantee is only as strong as the *set of routes* that reach the code it protects — and **nobody maintains that set.** `createChallan()` has a real invariant: *quantities must be positive.* That invariant is expressed in `createChallanSchema`, bolted to **one** of the **six** routes that reach the service. Add a seventh route tomorrow — a bulk import, a mobile endpoint, an internal job — and the invariant silently evaporates. **Nothing in the type system, the tests or the review process will notice**, because the invariant does not live anywhere near the thing it protects. **THIS IS THE SAME SHAPE AS TWO OTHER FINDINGS IN THIS REPORT**, which is what makes it a pattern rather than an anecdote: `approveStockCount` reaches `createStockAdjustment` **service-to-service**, bypassing `validateBody` entirely (BH-0318/BH-0342) — so the stock-adjustment *form* is blocked by a 400 while the *stock-count* path walks straight in. And the mandatory stock-sync rule is enforced by a pre-commit filter that misses 18 of 24 files (BH-0333). **In all three cases the rule is real, correct, and enforced somewhere that does not cover every caller.** THE FIX, IN ORDER OF DURABILITY: **(1)** Put the invariant in the **service**: `createChallan()` should itself reject a non-positive quantity, so no route can ever bypass it. **(2)** Put it in the **database**: a `CHECK (quantity > 0)` constraint holds no matter which code path writes — and you currently have **zero** check constraints across 576 money and quantity columns (BH-0301). **(3)** Keep `validateBody` for *shape and 400s*, which is what it is genuinely good at — turning a malformed request into a clean error rather than a 500. **Schema validation is a good front door. It is not a lock on the safe.**

A guarantee is therefore only as strong as the set of routes reaching the protected code — and nobody maintains that set

SAME SHAPE ELSEWHERE: approveStockCount reaches createStockAdjustment service-to-service, bypassing validateBody (BH-0318/BH-0342)
SAME SHAPE AGAIN: the stock-sync rule is enforced by a pre-commit filter covering 6 of 24 files (BH-0333)
FIX (1): invariants in the SERVICE — createChallan() rejects non-positive quantities itself
FIX (2): invariants in the DATABASE — CHECK (quantity > 0); you currently have ZERO check constraints across 576 columns
FIX (3): keep validateBody for shape/400s — that is what it is genuinely good for

Schema validation is a good front door; it is not a lock on the safe.
skeptic_verdict: CONFIRMED S2 — a synthesis, and the one that turns three separate findings into a single architectural instruction: move invariants down, to the service and the database, where every caller must pass through them.

title: THE VALIDATION EXPLICITLY PERMITS THE ONE VALUE THAT BREAKS THE MATH: shrinkage = 100% is allowed, and it divides by zero. And the live guard checks the WRONG END.
scenario:
MY FAVOURITE BUG OF THE RUN, because the schema and the formula are each individually reasonable and together they are lethal. **THE FORMULA** (used everywhere shrinkage is costed): `greigeRequired = fabricRequired / (1 - shrinkage/100)`. **THE SCHEMA:** `expectedShrinkagePercent: z.number().min(0).max(100)` (trimMasters.schema.ts:403), and identically `shrinkagePercent: z.number().min(0).max(100)` (fabricCosting.schema.ts:61). **`.max(100)` EXPLICITLY ALLOWS 100 — and `1 - 100/100 = 0`.** So the validator permits precisely the value that divides by zero. I ran the numbers:
```
shrinkage= 10%  ->  greigeRequired =   1,111.1
shrinkage= 50%  ->  greigeRequired =   2,000.0
shrinkage= 99%  ->  greigeRequired = 100,000.0     <- a 100x blowup
shrinkage=100%  ->  greigeRequired = Infinity
```
**AND THE LIVE GUARD IS AT THE WRONG BOUNDARY.** FabricCostingPage.tsx:1231 (and :2252) reads: `const greigeReq = shrinkage > 0 ? fabricReq / (1 - shrinkage / 100) : fabricReq;` — **it guards against 0 (which is harmless: 1/1 = 1) and permits 100 (which is catastrophic).** The check is on the wrong end of the range. **fabric_width_cad has 149 LIVE rows** — this is an actively-used screen. **THE REALISTIC FAILURE ISN'T MALICE, IT'S A KEYSTROKE.** Real shrinkage is 3-10%. Typing **`100` instead of `10`** — one extra zero — turns a 1,000 m requirement into **Infinity**; typing `90` instead of `9` turns it into **10,000 m instead of 1,099**. **There is no sanity ceiling anywhere**, so a fat-fingered shrinkage silently over-purchases by orders of magnitude. And downstream, `Math.max(0, Infinity - available)` faithfully propagates `Infinity` into the shortfall, into `costSheetPOGeneration.service.ts:386`, and finally into a **purchase-order line** — where writing `Infinity` to a Prisma `Decimal` throws an ORM error rather than a clean "shrinkage cannot be 100%" message. FIX: change `.max(100)` to `.lt(100)` (a 100% shrinkage is physically meaningless — the cloth would vanish), fix the live guard to check the upper bound rather than the lower, and add a sanity ceiling on shrinkage.

title: TWO MISSING REVERSALS: deleting a delivery note leaks finished-goods stock permanently, and approving a credit note never reduces what the customer owes
scenario: TWO SEPARATE REVERSAL BUGS, both found by asking what runs after the 400 is cleared. **(1) DELETING A DELIVERY NOTE PERMANENTLY LEAKS FINISHED-GOODS STOCK.** `createDeliveryNote` deducts `finished_goods_stock.quantity` **at creation** (dispatch.controller.ts:337-361) — not at dispatch. (`dispatchDeliveryNote` at :511 merely flips the status to IN_TRANSIT.) But `deleteDeliveryNote` (:390-411) is restricted to **PENDING** notes — **which have already had their stock deducted** — and it simply calls `prisma.delivery_notes.delete()` with **no restoration whatsoever.** So every deleted pending delivery note **destroys finished-goods stock permanently.** *(Note: `finished_goods_stock` is correctly outside the `material-sync` system — FG is not a raw material — so this is a genuine missing reversal, not a ledger-sync issue.)* **(2) APPROVING A CREDIT NOTE NEVER REDUCES THE INVOICE BALANCE.** `creditNote.service.ts:317-348 approve()` updates only `credit_notes.status = APPROVED`. It **never touches the parent invoice's `balanceAmount`, `paidAmount` or `status`** — I grepped: `invoice.service.ts` references `credit_notes` **only to block deletion** (:604-609), never to recompute a balance. **So issuing a credit note for a return or a quality claim does not reduce what the invoice says the customer owes.** The invoice keeps showing the full original amount as PENDING or OVERDUE — and that wrong figure then feeds your aging reports, your dashboards, and the **GSTR-1 CDNR section**. This is the same shape as the challan-cancel bug (BH-0214): a reversal that changes a status and reverses nothing. **ALSO (minor, same area):** `recordPayment` reads `paidAmount` and writes the new balance **without a transaction** (invoice.service.ts:627-698) — two concurrent payments on one invoice can race and silently drop one.

title: 🛑 SELF-CORRECTION #6: deleting the `status >= 500` retry clause is NOT enough — POSTs would still be retried on network errors, which is the case that actually duplicates data
scenario:
MY FIX WAS INCOMPLETE, AND IT LEAVES THE WORST CASE INTACT. I told you the duplicate-POST bug is fixed by deleting the `status >= 500` clause from the retry condition. Here is the actual config (api.ts:17-22):
```ts
retryCondition: (error) => (
  axiosRetry.isNetworkOrIdempotentRequestError(error) ||
  error.response?.status === 429 ||
  (error.response?.status !== undefined && error.response.status >= 500)
)
```
**Delete the third clause and the FIRST one still retries your POSTs.** `isNetworkOrIdempotentRequestError` is `isNetworkError(error) || isIdempotentRequestError(error)` — and **`isNetworkError` does not check the HTTP method.** It fires whenever there is **no response at all**: a dropped connection, a timeout, a flaky wifi hop. **And that is precisely the dangerous case** — the request may well have **succeeded on the server** and only the *response* was lost. Retrying it then creates a **second challan, a second stock movement, a second payment.** The `>= 500` case I told you to remove is actually the *less* dangerous one (a 500 usually means the write failed). **THE CORRECT FIX IS A METHOD GUARD, not a clause deletion:**
```ts
retryCondition: (error) =>
  error.config?.method?.toLowerCase() !== 'post' && ( ...existing conditions... )
```
**Never retry a POST. Full stop.** GET/HEAD/OPTIONS/PUT/DELETE are idempotent and safe to retry; POST is not. **My original advice would have left the duplicate-submission bug alive in exactly the scenario where it does the most damage.**

scenario: THE BOUND, and it is reassuring. The serializer applies **92 non-naive `RELATION_MAPPINGS`** — relations renamed to something other than their camelCase (e.g. `styleComponents -> components`, `grnItems -> items`, `purchaseOrderItems -> items`, `supplierContacts -> contacts`, `qualityDefects -> defects`). Each is a chance for the frontend to read the pre-map name and get `undefined`. **I swept the twelve most likely offenders — the short relation names that appear on live pages — and only two are actually misread:** `colorOptions` and `sizeOptions` (BH-0381). **The rest are CLEAN:** the frontend reads NONE of `.styleFabrics`, `.styleComponents`, `.styleProcesses`, `.purchaseOrderItems`, `.grnItems`, `.bomItems`, `.supplierContacts`, `.qualityDefects`, `.quotationItems`, or `.deliveryNoteItems` — it correctly uses the mapped names (`.fabrics`, `.components`, `.items`, etc.). And the naive raw-snake_case sweep (`.some_relation`) across every `.tsx` returned **only third-party XLSX calls** (`sheet_to_json`, `book_new`) — **zero raw snake_case relation reads.** **WHY THIS CLASS IS SMALL WHERE OTHERS WERE LARGE:** the serializer contract is old and well-worn — the frontend types encode the mapped names, and developers have hit this enough times to have internalised it (the CAD types file even documents it inline). The Zod-drift class was large because nothing enforced it; the serializer class is small because the mapped names are baked into the type definitions the whole frontend compiles against. **So `colorOptions`/`sizeOptions` are the exception, and they slipped through precisely because BOTH the naive AND mapped names are plausible English — a developer could write `colorOptions` from muscle memory and TypeScript would not complain if the style type declared it loosely.** CONCLUSION: one real finding, tightly bounded; the serializer layer is otherwise correctly consumed.
